summary: Polish-Jewish refugee and gulag survivor Peter Rachman became a Notting Hill slumlord in 1950s London, using thugs and racial tensions to drive out rent-protected tenants; after his 1962 death the press made his name a byword for abusive landlords.

evidence.note: Born to a Jewish family in Lviv, then Poland, in August 1919
Captured by Soviet forces and sent to forced forestry labour in Siberia
1941 Lviv pogrom, Janowska and Belzec as the likely fates of his family
Released under the Sikorski-Maisky deal, joins Anders Army via Tashkent and Iran
Polish Resettlement Corps in 1946; settles in Britain as a stateless resident
Soho underworld ties and a property office job from late 1950 start his landlording
Windrush arrivals, 1948 nationality law and the colour bar in London rentals
Former enforcers describe dogs, boxers and violent evictions in later court cases
1958 Notting Hill riots and how slum housing and the far right fed them
Falls ill after a casino night and dies in November 1962
1963 exposes and Profumo coverage scapegoat him once libel risk is gone
1964 Commons debate leads to the 1965 Rent Act and Race Relations Act

notes: Transcript spells the name Rockman; standard spelling Rachman used. Covered span ends 1965 with the laws passed in his name; the closing look at rent policy and today's UK housing shortage sets reaches_present. Origin lists UA (Lviv today) and PL (his nationality). Electoral politics (Labour using him against the Macmillan government) and his WWII army service get shorter segments and were left out of themes.
